forces: Trumpets, horns, oboes, bassoon, strings and continuo
performers: Marine Chamber Orchestra of the United States Marine Band; Major Michelle Rakers, conductor
intro: In the slow dance of the D major Water Music suite, trumpets and horns hold long notes beneath the oboes and violins. The brass rest during a middle strain, and then the opening returns.

sections.label: A · Lentement, oboes and violins
sections.mNote: Oboes and violins over held brass notes.

sections.label: A · First strain repeated
sections.mNote: The same nineteen bars, ending under a fermata.

sections.label: B · A strain without brass
sections.mNote: Oboes begin the new phrase; the strings join them.

sections.label: A · Return of the first strain
sections.mNote: The first strain returns once and closes on its fermata.

cues.title: Lentement, brass sustained notes
cues.text: Lentement means slowly. Oboes and violins play a tune in three beats, and beneath it trumpets and horns take turns holding long notes. The bass moves steadily, with figures that tell the continuo player which chords to supply.
cues.evidence: Samuel Arnold’s full score, The Celebrated Water-musick (1788), pp. 47–48: Lentement, 3/4, tied brass notes and figured bass. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_celebrated_Water-musick._In_score._Composed_in_the_year_1716._By_G._F._Handel_-_btv1b10072587v_(25_of_30).jpg
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second strain, woodwind and strings
cues.text: The second strain begins with oboes and bassoon, and the strings join their phrase. Trumpets and horns rest for fifteen bars. Woodwind and strings play the dance without the long brass notes.
cues.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 48–49; Lentement, bars 20–34 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe. The brass rest throughout the second strain. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_celebrated_Water-musick._In_score._Composed_in_the_year_1716._By_G._F._Handel_-_btv1b10072587v_(26_of_30).jpg
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Da capo return of the first strain
cues.text: Da capo brings back the opening strain, with the brass holding long notes. The final D major chord carries a fermata, and the mark Fine ends the movement there.
cues.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 48–49: opening strain’s fermata and second strain’s Da Capo; Hallische Händel-Ausgabe, bars 19 and 34, Fine and Da Capo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Fermata and repeat of the first strain
transitions.how: The first strain ends on a D major chord, with a fermata over every part. The repeat sign takes the players back to the upbeat. Oboes, strings and bass play the same tune again, and the trumpets and horns hold their long notes.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 47–48; Lentement, bar 19 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe: D major fermata chord and repeat sign.

transitions.title: Woodwinds after the D major fermata
transitions.how: The repeated strain ends on its D major fermata. Oboes and bassoon begin the next phrase while the strings rest, and the strings then join them. Trumpets and horns have no notes in this fifteen-bar strain, and the woodwinds play the opening alone.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 48–49; Lentement, bars 19–34 in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe: fermata, woodwind opening and rests in both brass parts.

transitions.title: Da capo, return of the brass
transitions.to: A · Return of the first strain
transitions.how: The second strain closes with oboes, strings and bass together. At the Da capo the orchestra goes back to the first upbeat and the D major opening, and the trumpets and horns play again. The first strain is repeated as far as the fermata chord, where the Fine ends the dance.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 48–49; Lentement, bar 34, Da Capo, and bar 19, the fermata and Fine, in the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe.

source.title: Handel, The Celebrated Water-musick in score (London: Samuel Arnold, 1788), pp. 47–49
source.locator: Arnold’s full score, pp. 47–49, Commons images 25–26. Bar numbers follow the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe, IV/13 (1962), pp. 51–52: first strain, bars 1–19, repeated; second strain, bars 20–34, without brass; da capo to Fine at bar 19.

timeline.note: Oboes and violins play the tune; trumpets and horns take turns holding long notes (bars 1–19).
The first strain is repeated with the same scoring.
Oboes and bassoon begin the second strain; strings join them while the brass rest (bars 20–34).
Da capo. The full scoring returns for the first strain, which is played once more.
Silence after the final D major chord.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Marine Chamber Orchestra, United States Marine Band (orchestra), Major Michelle A. Rakers (conductor)
fields.note: Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. This video’s frames show the conductor and the strings; the ensemble’s harpsichord, bassoon and trumpet are visible in the other movements’ videos, and no frame shows horns or oboes.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (14 of the three suites) and the structure heard (first strain of 19 bars played twice, second strain of 15 bars without brass, da capo to the fermata chord) match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
fields.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The structure follows from the measured silences and the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962), which prints 34 bars with a fermata, the mark Fine and a repeat sign at bar 19 and da capo at bar 34; IMSLP’s tally of 34 bars (53 with da capo) agrees.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Commons gives performance_date 2017-01-29; the programme prints Sunday, January 29, 2017 at 2:00 P.M.; the official video description repeats the date. The Handel group stands after the intermission in the programme. The Commons composition_date field, 1717-07-17, is the date of the documented first performance on the Thames, not a composition date.

composer.epithet: Composer who filled London theatres with Italian opera and later put an English-speaking chorus at the centre of the drama.
facts: Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; Hamburg’s opera orchestra; Italy, 1706–10
London from 1712; 25 Brook Street from 1723 until his death
British citizen from 1727; composer for the court, theatres and Foundling Hospital
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Handel was eighteen when he left Halle for Hamburg in 1703 and took a place in the opera orchestra. His father had been a barber-surgeon; his teacher Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow had taught him the organ, counterpoint and the habit of copying other people’s scores. He had enrolled at Halle’s university and worked as a church organist. Hamburg had a public theatre, singers to accompany and an audience that had bought tickets. His first opera, Almira, opened there in 1705, with German words and Italian arias.

In Italy he found patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Roman cardinals commissioned music from the young Protestant, and Prince Ruspoli provided him with singers and instrumentalists to write for. In the Dixit Dominus of 1707, a setting of a Latin psalm, five choral parts move at speed, then some voices hold dissonant notes while the others move underneath. He wrote chamber cantatas for a single singer. In Corelli’s Rome he learned to write for violin alongside the voice.
